## Current use

This energy assessment examines the current energy position of a brewery and identifies where the principal opportunities for improvement may lie. In terms of electricity, the brewery currently uses 3222 MWh per year, and it is clear from the breakdown of this consumption that refrigeration accounts for the largest share of the total. This is perhaps unsurprising, given the central role that cooling plays in the brewing process, but it does mean that any serious attempt to reduce electricity consumption at the site will need to focus primarily on the refrigeration systems and on the uses to which refrigeration is put.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration at the brewery serves a number of important duties. It is required for the control of fermentation temperatures, since the heat that is generated during fermentation has to be removed in order to hold the product at the temperature the process demands, and it is required for the cold storage of finished product prior to dispatch. It is also relevant to note that cold rooms and cellars lose cold continuously to their surroundings, so that the refrigeration plant is required to run even when production is not actively taking place. Taken together, these duties explain why refrigeration dominates the electricity consumption of the site, and why the way in which waste heat is handled elsewhere in the brewery is of such importance to the overall energy picture.

## Steam

Steam is used at the brewery for a variety of heating duties, including the heating of brewing liquor and the cleaning of vessels and pipework. It is, however, important to note an important limitation of the figures that are available in this area: the steam figures presented in this assessment are drawn from one winter month, and they therefore reflect the demands of the site during the colder part of the year rather than providing a balanced picture across the year as a whole. This seasonal aspect needs to be borne in mind whenever the steam figures are used, and it will be returned to in the recommendation below.

## Recommendation

The principal recommendation arising from this assessment concerns a heat-recovery retrofit. It is projected that the retrofit will save 15% of electricity use, which equates to a derived saving of 483 MWh per year. The capital cost of the retrofit is $339k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving works out at $57996, and the derived simple payback is 5.8 years. It is, however, essential to flag once again that the steam figures on which parts of this assessment rest are seasonal in nature, having been drawn from a single winter month, and for this reason the recommendation should be read with that qualification firmly in mind.

More broadly, it is worth reflecting on the fact that the pattern of consumption described above is by no means unusual for a brewery of this type. Brewing is an energy-intensive activity at both ends of the temperature scale: a great deal of heat is required in order to bring the brewing liquor and the wort to the temperatures that the process demands, and a great deal of cooling is subsequently required in order to bring the product back down again and to keep it cold thereafter. It is this combination of substantial heating duties and substantial cooling duties, existing side by side in the same process, that makes the question of heat recovery such a natural one to ask in the context of a brewery, since heat that is removed at one point in the process is, at least in principle, available to be used at another.

Looking ahead, it is clear that the refrigeration load will remain the dominant feature of the brewery's electricity consumption for the foreseeable future, since it is tied directly to the nature of the product and to the temperatures at which that product has to be held. Unless the scale of production changes materially, the proportions described in this assessment are unlikely to alter, and this stability in the pattern of consumption is itself relevant to the recommendation, because it means that a saving directed at the refrigeration-related loads is a saving directed at a load that will still be there, at a similar scale, for many years to come.

A final observation concerns the brewery's steam demand, which follows the rhythm of the brewing process itself. Because brewing takes place in batches, the demand for steam is not spread evenly across the working day but is instead concentrated into peaks associated with particular stages of the process, with quieter intervals in between. This pattern has practical implications for heat recovery, because heat that becomes available at a steady rate cannot always be absorbed by a demand that arrives in peaks, and some allowance for this mismatch may need to be made when the retrofit is designed in detail.

## Current use

The brewery uses 3222 MWh of electricity per year. Refrigeration takes the largest share of that total. The assessment therefore concentrates on refrigeration and on the heat that refrigeration rejects, because the largest saving available to the site stands in the relationship between the two: heat recovered from the refrigeration system displaces heat that the steam system would otherwise raise, and the electricity saving credited to heat recovery depends on where the refrigeration load falls.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration at the brewery covers fermentation cooling, wort cooling after the boil, and the cold storage of finished product. Fermentation cooling is a process load that follows the production schedule; cold storage is a standing load that continues whether or not production is running, because the stores lose cold to their surroundings continuously. The standing character of the storage load matters for heat recovery: a refrigeration plant that runs through the night and through shutdown periods rejects heat at times when the demand for recovered heat elsewhere in the brewery is at its lowest, and the value of the recovered heat depends on the coincidence of rejection and demand as much as on the quantity rejected.

## Steam

Steam serves the heating duties of the brewery: brewing liquor, the boil, and cleaning of vessels and pipework. The steam figures in this assessment come from one winter month. They describe the site under winter conditions, when space heating and the temperature of incoming water both raise steam demand, and they are not an average month. A steam balance built on these figures overstates the annual steam demand, and any saving calculated against that balance inherits the overstatement.

## Recommendation

A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 15% of electricity use, a derived saving of 483 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $339k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $57996 and the derived simple payback is 5.8 years. The recommendation is to proceed with the retrofit on these figures, with one qualification carried from the steam section: the steam figures are from one winter month and are seasonal, so the part of the case that rests on steam displacement should be re-examined against a full year of steam records before the design is fixed. The electricity saving and the payback stand on the electricity figures, which are annual; the seasonal qualification applies to the steam side of the assessment and does not change the payback as stated.

The structure of the electricity use also limits what an assessment can recommend. Because refrigeration dominates, measures aimed at the smaller electrical demands of the site, in lighting, in drives, and in office and ancillary loads, cannot move the annual total by more than a small amount even where they succeed completely. An assessment that distributes its recommendations evenly across all uses misrepresents the site: the refrigeration load is where the electricity is, and the refrigeration load is where the recoverable heat is, and the two facts together make heat recovery the natural centre of any programme for this brewery.

The rejected heat from refrigeration is not all equally available. Heat rejected at the condenser is at a temperature set by the condensing condition, and it can serve only those heating duties whose required temperature it can reach. Duties above that temperature still require steam, however much heat the refrigeration plant rejects. The retrofit case therefore depends on the brewery having enough demand at or below the rejection temperature, in the brewhouse, in cleaning, and in space and water heating, to absorb the recovered heat across the year rather than in a single season.

The steam section of an assessment is also where the brewery's operating pattern enters. Brewing is a batch process, and the steam demand of a batch process arrives in peaks at mashing, at the boil, and at cleaning, with quiet intervals between them. A heat-recovery system that delivers heat steadily meets a demand that arrives intermittently, and storage or a tolerance for wasting surplus heat at quiet times is part of the real design even where it is absent from the saving calculation. The annual figures in the recommendation are totals; they do not by themselves show how much of the recovered heat the brewery's daily pattern can actually absorb.

The qualification about the steam figures deserves its weight in the reading of this assessment. A single winter month is not a defective record of that month; it is an accurate record of the wrong period for annual conclusions. Steam raised in winter serves demands that shrink or vanish in summer, and the annual steam demand of the brewery is certainly lower than twelve times the winter figure. Any extension of the retrofit, beyond the electricity saving on which the recommendation rests, that is justified by steam displacement should wait for a full year of steam records, which the brewery can accumulate without capital spending and which would convert the weakest part of the present evidence into the strongest.
